A famous chef entered into a written agreement with his friend a well-known interior decorator respected for his unique designs in which the decorator agreed for a fixed fee to design the interior of the chef's new restaurant and upon the chef's approval of the design plan to decorate and furnish the restaurant accordingly. The agreement was silent as to assignment or delegation by either party. Before beginning the work the decorator sold his decorating business to Newman under an agreement in which the decorator assigned to Newman and Newman agreed to complete the chef-decorator contract. Newman also an experienced decorator of excellent repute advised the chef of the assignment and supplied him with information confirming both Newman's financial responsibility and past commercial success. Is the chef obligated to permit Newman to perform the chef-decorator agreement?

Choices:
A. Yes because the agreement contained no prohibition against assignment or delegation.
B. Yes because the chef received adequate assurances of Newman's ability to complete the job.
C. No because the decorator's duties were of a personal nature involving his reputation taste and skill.
D. No because the decorator's purported delegation to Newman of his obligations to the chef effected a novation.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Delegation of duties in contracts, specifically the rules governing when a contractual duty can be delegated to another party.

Fact Analysis: The chef-decorator agreement was silent on assignment or delegation, but the contract involved personal services including the decorator's unique taste and judgment in designing the interior of the chef's new restaurant. The decorator sold his business to Newman and assigned the contract to him, notifying the chef and providing assurances of Newman's capabilities.

Rule Application: A contractual duty can be delegated unless the other party to the contract has a substantial interest in having the original obligor perform. This substantial interest typically exists in personal services contracts where the obligee's taste and judgment are involved. Since the chef-decorator contract involved the decorator's personal taste and judgment, the chef has a substantial interest in having the decorator, not Newman, perform the contract.

Legal Conclusion: Given the personal nature of the decorator's duties and the chef's substantial interest in having the decorator perform, the decorator's delegation of the duty to Newman without the chef's consent amounts to a breach of contract. Therefore, the chef is not obligated to permit Newman to perform the contract, supporting option C.

A landholder was land-rich by inheritance but money-poor having suffered severe losses on bad investments but still owned several thousand acres of unencumbered timberland. He had a large family and his normal fixed personal expenses were high. Pressed for cash he advertised a proposed sale of standing timber on a choice 2000-acre tract. The only response was an offer by a logger the owner of a large integrated construction enterprise after inspection of the advertised tract. The logger offered a fair price for the timber rights in question and the landholder accepted the offer. The 2000-acre tract was an abundant wild-game habitat and had been used for many years with the landholder's permission by area hunters. The logger's performance of the timber contract would destroy this habitat. Without legal excuse and over the landholder's strong objection the logger repudiated the contract before commencing performance. The landholder could not afford to hire a lawyer and take legal action and made no attempt to assign any cause of action he might have had against the logger. If the logger is sued for breach of the contract by the landholder's next-door neighbor whose view of a nearby lake is obscured by the standing timber the neighbor will probably

Choices:
A. lose as only an incidental beneficiary if any of the logger-landholder contract.
B. lose as a maintainer of nuisance litigation.
C. prevail as a third-party intended beneficiary of the logger-landholder contract.
D. prevail as a surrogate for the landholder in view of his inability to enforce the contract.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Third-party beneficiary rights in contract law, specifically the requirements for a third party to have standing to enforce a promise.

Fact Analysis: The logger and the landholder entered into a contract for the sale of timber rights on a 2000-acre tract. The logger repudiated the contract before commencing performance, which would have destroyed a wild-game habitat used by area hunters and also affected the view of the landholder's next-door neighbor. The neighbor seeks to sue the logger for breach of contract.

Rule Application: A third party can enforce a promise only if they are an intended beneficiary, which requires that the parties intended to confer a benefit on the beneficiary. The neighbor's potential benefit from the contract's performance (improved view) does not establish intent by the parties to confer a benefit on the neighbor, making them merely an incidental beneficiary without standing to enforce the contract.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the neighbor lacks the necessary intent from the parties to be considered an intended beneficiary, they do not have standing to enforce the logger-landholder contract. Therefore, the neighbor will probably lose the lawsuit, supporting option A.

A fixtures company in a signed writing contracted with an apartment complex for the sale to the apartment complex of 50 identical sets of specified bathroom fixtures 25 sets to be delivered on March 1 and the remaining 25 sets on April 1. The agreement did not specify the place of delivery or the time or place of payment. On March 1 the fixtures company tendered 24 sets to the apartment complex and explained "One of the 25 sets was damaged in transit from the manufacturer to us but we will deliver a replacement within 5 days." Which of the following statements is correct?

Choices:
A. The apartment complex is entitled to accept any number of the 24 sets reject the rest and cancel the contract both as to any rejected sets and the lot due on April 1.
B. The apartment complex is entitled to accept any number of the 24 sets and to reject the rest but is not entitled to cancel the contract as to any rejected sets or the lot due on April 1.
C. The apartment complex must accept the 24 sets but is entitled to cancel the rest of the contract.
D. The apartment complex must accept the 24 sets and is not entitled to cancel the rest of the contract.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Installment contracts under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically the buyer's obligations regarding non-conforming installments.

Fact Analysis: The fixtures company contracted to deliver 50 sets of bathroom fixtures to the apartment complex in two installments. On the first delivery date, the company tendered 24 sets, explaining that one set was damaged in transit and promising a replacement within five days.

Rule Application: Under the UCC, an installment contract allows for the delivery of goods in separate lots to be separately accepted. If an installment is non-conforming, the buyer must accept it if the seller gives adequate assurance of curing the defect, unless the non-conformity substantially impairs the value of the installment and cannot be cured.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the fixtures company-apartment complex contract is an installment contract and the fixtures company provided adequate assurance of curing the defect by promising a replacement within five days, the apartment complex must accept the 24 sets and is not entitled to cancel the rest of the contract, supporting option D.

On March 1 a mechanic contracted to repair a textile company's knitting machine and to complete the job by March 6. On March 2 the textile company contracted to manufacture and deliver specified cloth to a knitwear company on March 15. The textile company knew that it would have to use the machine then under repair to perform this contract. Because the knitwear company order was for a rush job the knitwear company and the textile company included in their contract a liquidated damages clause providing that the textile company would pay $5000 for each day's delay in delivery after March 15. The mechanic was inexcusably five days late in repairing the machine and as a result the textile company was five days late in delivering the cloth to the knitwear company. The textile company paid $25000 to the knitwear company as liquidated damages and now sues the mechanic for $25000. Both the mechanic and the textile company knew when making their contract on March 1 that under ordinary circumstances the textile company would sustain little or no damages of any kind as a result of a five-day delay in the machine repair. Assuming that the $5000 liquidated damages clause in the knitwear-textile contract is valid which of the following arguments will serve as the mechanic's best defense to the textile company's action?

Choices:
A. Time was not of the essence in the mechanic-textile contract.
B. The mechanic had no reason to foresee on March 1 that the knitwear company would suffer consequential damages in the amount of $25000.
C. By entering into the knitwear company contract while knowing that its knitting machine was being repaired the textile company assumed the risk of any delay's loss to the knitwear company.
D. In all probability the liquidated damages paid by the textile company to the knitwear company are not the same amount as the actual damages sustained by the knitwear company in consequence of the textile company's late delivery of the cloth.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Damages for breach of contract, specifically the foreseeability of consequential damages at the time of contract formation.

Fact Analysis: The mechanic contracted to repair the textile company's knitting machine by March 6, and the textile company had a separate contract with the knitwear company that included a liquidated damages clause for late delivery. The mechanic was five days late, resulting in the textile company paying $25,000 in liquidated damages to the knitwear company.

Rule Application: Damages for breach of contract are limited to losses that the breaching party had reason to foresee as a probable result of the breach at the time the contract was made. In this case, neither the mechanic nor the textile company was aware of the textile company's prospective liability under its contract with the knitwear company at the time of their contract.

Legal Conclusion: Because the mechanic did not have reason to foresee the $25,000 loss the textile company sustained due to the mechanic's breach, the loss is not recoverable as an element of damages, supporting option B.

A written construction contract under which a contractor agreed to build a new house for an owner at a fixed price of $200000 contained the following provision: Prior to construction or during the course thereof this contract may be modified by mutual agreement of the parties as to "extras" or other departures from the plans and specifications provided by the owner and attached hereto. Such modifications however may be authorized only in writing signed by both parties. During construction the contractor incorporated into the structure overhanging gargoyles and other "extras" orally requested by the owner for orally agreed prices in addition to the contract price. The owner subsequently refused to pay anything for such extras aggregating $30000 at the agreed prices solely on the ground that no written signed authorization for them was ever effected. If the contractor sues the owner on account of the "extras" which if any of the following will effectively support the owner's defense? I. The parol evidence rule. II. The preexisting duty rule. III. Failure of an express condition. IV. The statute of frauds.

Choices:
A. I and III only.
B. I and IV only.
C. II and IV only.
D. Neither I II III nor IV

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Enforceability of contract modifications, specifically the role of no-oral-modification clauses in construction contracts.

Fact Analysis: The owner-contractor agreement included a provision requiring any modifications to be made in writing and signed by both parties. Despite this, the owner orally requested and agreed on prices for extras, which the contractor incorporated into the structure.

Rule Application: A no-oral-modification clause can be enforceable, but it may not bar recovery if the contractor has relied on the owner's verbal request. In this case, the contractor's incorporation of the extras based on the owner's oral request may constitute reliance, potentially undermining the enforceability of the no-oral-modification clause.

Legal Conclusion: Given the contractor's reliance on the owner's verbal request for extras, none of the provided options (parol evidence rule, preexisting duty rule, failure of an express condition, or the statute of frauds) effectively support the owner's defense against paying for the extras, leading to the conclusion that none of the options are correct.

On April 1 an owner and a buyer signed a writing in which the owner in consideration of $100 to be paid to the owner by the buyer offered the buyer the right to purchase Greenacre for $100000 within 30 days. The writing further provided "This offer will become effective as an option only if and when the $100 consideration is in fact paid." On April 20 the owner having received no payment or other communication from the buyer sold and conveyed Greenacre to a citizen for $120000. On April 21 the owner received a letter from the buyer enclosing a cashier's check for $100 payable to the owner and stating "I am hereby exercising my option to purchase Greenacre and am prepared to close whenever you're ready." Which of the following if proved best support the buyer's suit against the owner for breach of contract?

Choices:
A. The buyer was unaware of the sale to the citizen when the owner received the letter and check from the buyer on April 21.
B. On April 15 the buyer decided to purchase Greenacre and applied for and obtained a commitment from a bank for a $75000 loan to help finance the purchase.
C. When the April 1 writing was signed the owner said to the buyer "Don't worry about the $100; the recital of '$100 to be paid' makes this deal binding."
D. The owner and the buyer are both professional dealers in real estate.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Option contracts and the requirements for their enforceability, including consideration and revocation.

Fact Analysis: The owner and buyer signed a writing on April 1, which included an offer for the buyer to purchase Greenacre within 30 days, contingent on the payment of $100 consideration. The owner sold Greenacre to a third party on April 20 without receiving payment or communication from the buyer. The buyer then sent a letter and cashier's check for $100 on April 21, exercising the option to purchase.

Rule Application: An option promise requires consideration to be enforceable, but the offer can still be accepted by the offeree unless it lapses or the offeree receives notice of revocation. Since the consideration had not been paid, the owner's April 1 letter was not effective as an option at the time of the conveyance to the citizen. However, the offer did not lapse until April 30, leaving the buyer free to accept unless they received notice of the conveyance.

Legal Conclusion: The buyer's lack of awareness of the sale to the citizen when the owner received the letter and check on April 21 is crucial, as it indicates the buyer did not receive notice of revocation. This supports the buyer's suit against the owner for breach of contract, making option A the correct answer.

On June 1 a seller and a buyer contracted in writing for the sale and purchase of the seller's cattle ranch (a large single tract) and to close the transaction on December 1. The buyer unequivocally repudiated the contract on August 1. On August 15 the seller urged the buyer to change her mind and proceed with the scheduled closing on December 1. On October 1 having heard nothing further from the buyer the seller sold and conveyed his ranch to a rancher without notice to the buyer. On December 1 the buyer attempted to close under the June 1 contract by tendering the full purchase price to the seller. The seller rejected the tender. If the buyer sues the seller for breach of contract the buyer will probably

Choices:
A. win because the seller failed to seasonably notify the buyer of any pending sale to the rancher.
B. win because the seller waived the buyer's August 1 repudiation by urging her to retract it on August 15.
C. lose because the buyer did not retract her repudiation before the seller materially changed his position in reliance thereon by selling the ranch to the rancher.
D. lose because acceptance of the purchase price by the seller was a concurrent condition to the seller's obligation to convey the ranch to the buyer on December 1.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Contract law, specifically the effect of repudiation and the right to terminate or retract repudiation.

Fact Analysis: The buyer unequivocally repudiated the contract on August 1, but later attempted to retract the repudiation on December 1 by tendering the full purchase price. Meanwhile, the seller urged the buyer to change her mind on August 15, but ultimately sold and conveyed the ranch to a rancher on October 1 without notice to the buyer.

Rule Application: A repudiation gives the non-repudiating party the right to terminate the contract if it deprives them of a substantial part of the contract. However, the repudiating party can retract the repudiation if done before the non-repudiating party materially relies on the repudiation or indicates it is final. In this case, the seller materially relied on the repudiation by selling the ranch to a rancher on October 1.

Legal Conclusion: Since the seller had already materially relied on the repudiation by conveying the ranch to the rancher on October 1, the buyer's attempted retraction on December 1 was not timely. Therefore, the buyer will probably lose the suit for breach of contract, supporting option C.

A computer company contracted in writing with a bank to sell and deliver to the bank a mainframe computer using a new type of magnetic memory then under development but not perfected by the computer company at a price substantially lower than that of a similar computer using current technology. The contract's delivery term was "F.O.B. the bank on or before July 31." After making the contract with the bank the computer company discovered that the new technology it intended to use was unreliable and that no computer manufacturer could yet build a reliable computer using that technology. The computer company thereupon notified the bank that it was impossible for the computer company or anyone else to build the contracted-for computer "in the present state of the art." If the bank sues the computer company for failure to perform its computer contract the court will probably decide the case in favor of

Choices:
A. the computer company because its performance of the contract was objectively impossible.
B. the computer company because a contract to build a machine using technology under development imposes only a duty on the builder to use its best efforts to achieve the result contracted for.
C. the bank because the law of impossibility does not apply to merchants under the applicable law.
D. the bank because the computer company assumed the risk in the given circumstances that the projected new technology would not work reliably.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Impracticability as a defense to breach of contract under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically the assumption of risk by the seller.

Fact Analysis: The computer company contracted to sell and deliver a mainframe computer using a new, unperfected magnetic memory technology at a lower price than current technology. After contracting, the company discovered the technology was unreliable and notified the bank that it was impossible to build the computer as agreed.

Rule Application: Under the UCC, a seller's performance is excused if it becomes impracticable due to an event that was a basic assumption of the contract, unless the event was sufficiently foreshadowed and thus a risk assumed by the seller. Here, the computer company was aware the technology was not yet perfected when it entered the contract, indicating it assumed the risk of the technology's unreliability.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the computer company was aware of the risks associated with the new technology and contracted to deliver a product based on it, the court will likely decide in favor of the bank, as the computer company's failure to perform is not excused by impracticability. This supports option D.

A manager aged 60 who had no plans for early retirement had worked for an insurance company for 20 years as a managerial employee-at-will when he had a conversation with the company's president about the manager's post-retirement goal of extensive travel around the United States. A month later the president handed the manager a written signed resolution of the company's Board of Directors stating that when and if the manager should decide to retire at his option the company in recognition of his past service would pay him a $2000-per-month lifetime pension. (The company had no regularized retirement plan for at-will employees.) Shortly thereafter the manager retired and immediately bought a $30000 recreational vehicle for his planned travels. After receiving the promised $2000 monthly pension from the insurance company for six months the manager now unemployable elsewhere received a letter from the insurance company advising him that the pension would cease immediately because of recessionary budget constraints affecting in varying degrees all managerial salaries and retirement pensions. In a suit against the insurance company for breach of contract the manager will probably

Choices:
A. win because he retired from the company as bargained-for consideration for the Board's promise to him of a lifetime pension.
B. win because he timed his decision to retire and to buy the recreational vehicle in reasonable reliance on the Board's promise to him of a lifetime pension.
C. lose because the Board's promise to him of a lifetime pension was an unenforceable gift promise.

Rule Application: A gratuitous promise may be enforceable under the theory of detrimental reliance if the promisor had reason to expect reliance, there was actual reliance, and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice. A breeder bought a two-month-old registered boar at auction from a seller for $800. No express warranty was made. Fifteen months later tests by experts proved conclusively that the boar had been born incurably sterile. Which of the following will the court probably decide?

B. The breeder wins because the seller impliedly warranted that the boar was fit for breeding.

D. The seller wins because any mistake involved was unilateral not mutual.

Legal Concept: Rescission of a contract due to mutual mistake of fact, specifically regarding the fertility of a boar.

Fact Analysis: The breeder purchased a two-month-old registered boar from the seller for $800, with no express warranty made. Fifteen months later, it was discovered that the boar was incurably sterile, significantly reducing its value. Rule Application: A contract can be rescinded due to mutual mistake if the mistake is fundamental to the contract and has a material effect on the exchange. However, if the court determines that one party should bear the risk of the mistake, rescission may not be allowed. In this case, the mistake about the boar's fertility had a significant impact on its value, but the breeder was aware of the possibility of infertility at the time of purchase.

A bakery offered a chef a permanent full-time job as a pastry chef at a salary of $2000 per month. The chef agreed to take the position and to begin work in two weeks. One week after the chef was hired by the bakery a hotel offered the chef a position as a restaurant manager at a salary of $2500 a month. A bottling company sent a purchase order to a wholesaler that stated "Ship 100000 empty plastic bottles at the posted price." Two days after receipt of this purchase order the wholesaler shipped the bottles and the bottling company accepted delivery of them. A week after the bottles were delivered the bottling company received the wholesaler's acknowledgement form which included a provision disclaiming consequential damages. After using the bottles for two months the bottling company discovered a defect in the bottles that caused its products to leak from them. The bottling company recalled 10000 of the bottles containing its product incurring lost profits of $40000. Assuming all appropriate defenses are seasonably raised will the bottling company succeed in recovering $40000 in consequential damages from the wholesaler?

Choices:
A. No because buyers are generally not entitled to recover consequential damages.
B. No because the bottling company's acceptance of the goods also constituted an acceptance of the terms included in the wholesaler's acknowledgement.
C. Yes because the disclaimer of consequential damages is unconscionable.
D. Yes because the wholesaler's acknowledgement did not alter the terms of an existing contract between the parties.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Contract formation and terms under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically the acceptance of goods and the inclusion of terms in a contract.

Fact Analysis: The bottling company sent a purchase order for 100000 empty plastic bottles at the posted price, which the wholesaler accepted by shipping the bottles two days later. The bottling company accepted delivery of the bottles. A week later, the wholesaler sent an acknowledgement form that included a provision disclaiming consequential damages.

Rule Application: Under UCC § 2-206, an offer to buy goods for prompt shipment is accepted when the seller ships the goods. Therefore, the contract was formed when the wholesaler shipped the bottles, and its terms consisted of the negotiated terms plus UCC gap-fillers. The subsequent acknowledgement form with additional terms, including the disclaimer of consequential damages, was an ineffective attempt to modify the contract terms, which were not accepted by the buyer.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the contract was formed upon shipment and the acknowledgement form's proposed modifications were not accepted, the bottling company is entitled to recover consequential damages. The correct answer is D, as the wholesaler's acknowledgement did not alter the terms of the existing contract between the parties.

A mother whose adult son was a law school graduate contracted with a tutor to give the son a bar exam preparation course. "If my son passes the bar exam" the mother explained to the tutor "he has been promised a job with a law firm that will pay $55000 a year." The tutor agreed to do the work for $5000 although the going rate was $6000. Before the instruction was to begin the tutor repudiated the contract. Although the mother or the son reasonably could have employed for $6000 an equally qualified instructor to replace the tutor neither did so. The son failed the bar exam and the law firm refused to employ him. It can be shown that had the son received the instruction he would have passed the bar exam. If the mother and the son join as parties plaintiff and sue the tutor for breach of contract how much if anything are they entitled to recover?

Choices:
A. $1000 because all other damages could have been avoided by employing another equally qualified instructor.
B. $55000 because damages of that amount were within the contemplation of the parties at the time they contracted.
C. Nominal damages only because the mother was not injured by the breach and the tutor made no promise to the son.
D. Nothing because neither the mother nor the son took steps to avoid the consequences of the tutor's breach.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Mitigation of damages in contract law, specifically the principle that a victim of a breach is entitled to recover only those damages which could not reasonably have been avoided.

Fact Analysis: The tutor repudiated the contract to provide bar exam preparation for the son, and despite the mother and son's ability to hire an equally qualified instructor for $6000, they failed to do so. The son subsequently failed the bar exam and lost the promised job.

Rule Application: The rule of mitigation of damages requires that the victims of a breach take reasonable steps to avoid or minimize damages. However, failure to mitigate does not preclude recovery of damages measured by the difference between contract and market price. In this case, the mother and son could have avoided additional damages by hiring a substitute teacher for $6000, which is only $1000 more than the original contract price.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the mother and son could have reasonably avoided further damages by hiring a substitute teacher for $6000, they are entitled to recover the difference between the contract price and the market price, which is $1000. This amount is necessary to put them in the position they would have been in had the contract been performed, supporting option A.

B. No because the contract called for a loan at an interest rate not to exceed 10% and it could not be modified without the consent of the seller.
C. Yes because the buyer detrimentally changed position in reliance on the seller's promise to convey.

Fact Analysis: The buyer and seller entered into a contract for the sale of land, with the buyer's obligation to purchase conditioned on obtaining a loan at an interest rate no higher than 10%. The buyer was unable to secure such a loan but obtained one at 10.5% and tendered the purchase price. The seller refused to perform, citing the increased value of the land.

A carpenter contracted with a homeowner to remodel the homeowner's home for $10000 to be paid on completion of the work. On May 29 relying on his expectation that he would finish the work and have the homeowner's payment on June 1 the carpenter contracted to buy a car for "$10000 in cash if payment is made on June 1; if payment is made thereafter the price is $12000." The carpenter completed the work according to specifications on June 1 and demanded payment from the homeowner on that date. The homeowner without any excuse refused to pay. Thereupon the carpenter became very excited suffered a minor heart attack and as a result incurred medical expenses of $1000. The reasonable value of the carpenter's services in remodeling the homeowner's home was $13000. In an action by the carpenter against the homeowner which of the following should be the carpenter's measure of recovery?

Choices:
A. $10000 the contract price.
B. $11000 the contract price plus $1000 for the medical expenses incurred because the homeowner refused to pay.
C. $12000 the contract price plus $2000 the bargain that was lost because the carpenter could not pay cash for the car on June 1.
D. $13000 the amount the homeowner was enriched by the carpenter's services.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Contract law, specifically the measure of recovery for a contractor when a homeowner breaches the contract by failing to pay for completed work.

Fact Analysis: The carpenter completed the remodeling work as agreed upon for a contract price of $10000, but the homeowner refused to pay without excuse. The carpenter had relied on timely payment to purchase a car and as a result of the breach, incurred medical expenses and lost a bargain.

Rule Application: The general rule in contract law is that a contractor is entitled to the contract price for work completed when a homeowner breaches by failing to pay. Additional damages such as medical expenses incurred due to the breach or lost bargains are typically unrecoverable if they were unforeseeable at the time the contract was made or not directly caused by the breach. Furthermore, an unjust enrichment claim cannot exceed the contract price when all work is completed and only payment remains.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the carpenter completed the work as agreed and the homeowner's breach did not directly cause the additional damages claimed, the carpenter's measure of recovery should be the contract price of $10000, supporting option A.

A buyer and a seller entered into a contract for the sale of 10000 novelty bracelets. The seller had the bracelets in stock. The contract specified that the seller would ship the bracelets by a third-party carrier. However the contract did not specify either who was to pay the costs of carriage or the place of tender for the bracelets. On the above facts when would the risk of loss of the bracelets pass to the buyer?

Choices:
A. When the contract was made.
B. When the bracelets were identified to the contract by the seller assuming the goods conformed to the contract.
C. When the bracelets were delivered to a carrier and a proper contract for their carriage was made.
D. When the bracelets were unloaded on the buyer's premises by the carrier.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Passage of risk of loss in a shipment contract under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically when the contract requires the seller to ship goods to the buyer by a third-party carrier.

Fact Analysis: The contract between the buyer and seller for the sale of novelty bracelets specified shipment by a third-party carrier but did not specify who was to pay the costs of carriage or the place of tender for the bracelets. The seller had the bracelets in stock.

Rule Application: Under UCC § 2-509(1), a contract requiring shipment by a third-party carrier is presumed to be a shipment contract if the contract is silent on the matter. According to Comment 5 to UCC § 2-503, in a shipment contract, the risk of loss passes from the seller to the buyer when the seller duly delivers the goods to the third-party carrier.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the contract is a shipment contract and the seller duly delivered the goods to the third-party carrier, the risk of loss of the bracelets would pass to the buyer at the time of delivery to the carrier, supporting option C.

In a written contract an architect agreed to draw up the plans for and to supervise construction of a client's new house. In return the client agreed to pay the architect a fee of $10000 to be paid upon the house's completion. After completion the client claimed erroneously but in good faith that the architect's plans were defective. The client orally offered to pay the architect $7500 in full settlement of the claim for the fee. The architect orally accepted that offer despite the fact that the reasonable value of his services was in fact $10000. The client paid the architect $7500 pursuant to their agreement. The architect subsequently sued the client for the remaining $2500. In a preliminary finding the trier of fact found that there were no defects in the architect's plans. Will the architect be likely to prevail in his action against the client for $2500?

Choices:
A. Yes because payment of $7500 cannot furnish consideration for the architect's promise to surrender his claim.
B. Yes because the oral agreement to modify the written contract is not enforceable.
C. No because the architect's promise to accept $7500 became binding when the client made the payment.
D. No because the architect's acceptance of partial payment constituted a novation.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Accord and satisfaction in contract law, specifically the requirements for a valid accord and the effect of satisfaction on the original debt.

Fact Analysis: The architect and the client had a written contract for $10,000, but the client claimed in good faith that the architect's plans were defective and offered to pay $7,500 in full settlement. The architect accepted this offer orally, despite the fact that his services were worth $10,000. The client then paid the $7,500, and the architect later sued for the remaining $2,500.

Rule Application: An accord requires consideration, but this consideration can be less than what was originally promised. Payment of a lesser amount on a valid claim can be valid consideration if there is a bona fide dispute about the amount owed, made in good faith. In this case, the client's good faith dispute about the architect's fee provided the necessary consideration for the accord. The architect's acceptance of the $7,500 payment constituted satisfaction, which discharges both the accord and the original debt.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the architect's agreement to accept $7,500 was supported by consideration due to the good faith dispute, and that the payment of $7,500 constituted satisfaction, the architect is unlikely to prevail in his action against the client for the remaining $2,500. This supports option C.

On June 1 a seller agreed in a writing signed by both the seller and the buyer to sell an antique car to a buyer for $20000. The car was at the time on display in a museum in a different city and was to be delivered to the buyer on August 1. On July 15 before the risk of loss had passed to the buyer the car was destroyed by fire without fault of either party. Subsequent to the contract but before the fire the car had increased in value to $30000. The seller sued the buyer for the contract price of $20000 and the buyer counterclaimed for $30000. Which of the following will the court conclude?

Choices:
A. Both claims fail.
B. Only the seller's claim prevails.
C. Only the buyer's claim prevails.
D. Both claims prevail.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Avoidance of contract due to destruction of goods under UCC § 2-613 and the effect on performance obligations.

Fact Analysis: The contract specified the sale of a particular antique car, which was identified at the time of contract formation. The car was destroyed by fire before the risk of loss had passed to the buyer and without fault of either party.

Rule Application: UCC § 2-613 states that if identified goods are totally destroyed before the risk of loss has passed to the buyer and without the fault of either party, the contract is avoided. UCC § 2-501 confirms that the goods were identified at contract formation. Since the conditions for avoidance are met, both parties are relieved of their performance obligations.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the contract is avoided due to the destruction of the goods, neither party can assert a valid claim against the other. Therefore, both the seller's claim for the contract price and the buyer's counterclaim for the increased value of the car fail, supporting option A.

A homeowner and a contractor entered into a contract for the construction of a home for the price of $300000. The contractor was to earn a profit of $10000 for the job. After the contractor had spent $45000 on labor and materials including $5000 on oak flooring not yet installed the homeowner informed the contractor that the homeowner had lost his job and could not pay for any services. The homeowner told the contractor to stop working immediately. The reasonable market value of the labor and materials provided by the contractor at that point including the oak flooring was $40000. The contractor used the $5000 worth of oak flooring on another job. In an action by the contractor against the homeowner for damages which of the following would be the largest amount of damages recoverable by the contractor?

Choices:
A. $40000 the reasonable value of the services the contractor had provided.
B. $40000 the contractor's construction costs.
C. $50000 the contractor's construction costs of $45000 plus the $10000 profit minus the $5000 saved by reusing the oak flooring on another job.
D. $55000 the contractor's construction costs of $45000 plus the $10000 profit.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Contract law, specifically the calculation of damages for breach of contract in a construction agreement.

Fact Analysis: The contractor had spent $45000 on labor and materials, including $5000 on oak flooring not yet installed, when the homeowner breached the contract by informing the contractor to stop working due to financial difficulties. The reasonable market value of the labor and materials provided, including the oak flooring, was $40000. The contractor reused the oak flooring on another job, saving $5000.

Rule Application: In a breach of contract case, the contractor is entitled to recover damages that will put them in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed. This includes the contractor's construction costs, plus any expected profit, minus any savings or benefits realized due to the breach. Here, the contractor's construction costs were $45000, with an expected profit of $10000, and they saved $5000 by reusing the oak flooring.

Legal Conclusion: The largest amount of damages recoverable by the contractor would be $50000, which is the contractor's construction costs of $45000 plus the $10000 profit, minus the $5000 saved by reusing the oak flooring on another job, supporting option C.

On June 1 a seller received a mail order from a buyer requesting prompt shipment of a specified computer model at the seller's current catalog price. On June 2 the seller mailed to the buyer a letter accepting the order and assuring the buyer that the computer would be shipped on June 3. On June 3 the seller realized that he was out of that computer model and shipped to the buyer a different computer model and a notice of accommodation. On June 5 the buyer received the seller's June 2 letter and the different computer model but not the notice of accommodation. At that juncture which of the following is a correct statement of the parties' legal rights and duties?

Choices:
A. The buyer can either accept or reject the different computer model and in either event recover damages if any for breach of contract.
B. The buyer can either accept or reject the different computer model but if he rejects it he will thereby waive any remedy for breach of contract.
C. The seller's prompt shipment of nonconforming goods constituted an acceptance of the buyer's offer thereby creating a contract for sale of the replacement computer model.
D. The seller's notice of accommodation was timely mailed and his shipment of the different computer model constituted a counteroffer.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Contract formation and performance under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically the acceptance of offers and the shipment of nonconforming goods.

Fact Analysis: The seller accepted the buyer's offer by mailing a letter of acceptance on June 2, promising to ship the specified computer model. However, the seller shipped a different computer model on June 3, along with a notice of accommodation, which the buyer received on June 5.

Rule Application: UCC § 2-206(1)(b) provides that a contract calling for prompt shipment can be accepted by either a prompt promise to ship or by the prompt shipment of goods. The seller's June 2 letter constituted an acceptance of the buyer's offer. UCC § 2-601 allows a buyer to accept or reject nonconforming goods and in either event recover damages.

Legal Conclusion: Since the seller's shipment of the different computer model constituted a breach of contract, the buyer has the right to either accept or reject the nonconforming goods and, in either event, recover damages for breach of contract, supporting option A.

A debtor's liquidated and undisputed $1000 debt to a creditor was due on March 1. On March 15 the creditor told the debtor that if the debtor promised to pay the $1000 on or before December 1 then the creditor wouldn't sue to collect the debt. The debtor orally agreed. On April 1 the creditor sued the debtor to collect the debt that had become due on March 1. The debtor moved to dismiss the creditor's complaint. Should the court grant the debtor's motion?

Choices:
A. No because there was no consideration to support the creditor's promise not to sue.
B. No because there was no consideration to support the debtor's promise to pay $1000 on December 1.
C. Yes because a promise to allow a debtor to delay payment on a past debt is enforceable without consideration.
D. Yes because the debtor was bargaining for the creditor's forbearance.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Consideration in contract law, specifically the pre-existing duty rule and its application to debt settlement agreements.

Fact Analysis: The creditor and debtor entered into an oral agreement where the creditor would not sue for the debt if the debtor promised to pay the undisputed $1000 by December 1, despite the debt being due on March 1.

Rule Application: For a settlement to be enforceable, consideration is required. The pre-existing duty rule states that a promise to perform a pre-existing duty is not sufficient consideration to support a return promise. In this case, the debtor's promise to pay the $1000 by December 1 was merely a promise to perform a pre-existing duty, as the amount was already due and undisputed.

Legal Conclusion: Since the creditor's promise to forbear from suing was not supported by consideration from the debtor, the agreement is not enforceable. Therefore, the court should not grant the debtor's motion to dismiss the creditor's complaint, supporting option A.

On March 1 a homeowner contacted a builder about constructing an addition to the homeowner's house. The builder orally offered to perform the work for $200000 if his pending bid on another project was rejected. The homeowner accepted the builder's terms and the builder then prepared a written contract that both parties signed. The contract did not refer to the builder's pending bid. One week later upon learning that his pending bid on the other project had been accepted the builder refused to perform any work for the homeowner. Can the homeowner recover for the builder's nonperformance?

Choices:
A. No because efficiency principles justify the builder's services being directed to a higher-valued use.
B. No because the builder's duty to perform was subject to a condition.
C. Yes because the builder's attempt to condition his duty to perform rendered the contract illusory.
D. Yes because the parol evidence rule would bar the builder from presenting evidence of oral understandings not included in the final writing.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: The parol evidence rule and its exceptions, particularly the condition exception, in contract law.

Fact Analysis: The builder orally offered to perform work for the homeowner contingent on his pending bid on another project being rejected. The homeowner accepted, and a written contract was signed without referencing the pending bid. The builder later refused to perform upon learning his bid on the other project was accepted.

Rule Application: The parol evidence rule generally bars evidence of prior negotiations or agreements that contradict, modify, or vary contractual terms if the contract is intended to be complete and final. However, an exception allows extrinsic evidence to establish an oral condition to performance. Here, the builder's performance was conditioned on his bid being rejected, an oral condition not included in the written contract.

Legal Conclusion: Since the builder's bid was accepted, the condition for his performance did not occur, and thus he is not in breach of the contract. Therefore, the homeowner cannot recover for the builder's nonperformance, supporting option B.

A collector bought from a gallery a painting correctly described in the parties' signed contract as a "one-of-a-kind self-portrait" by a famous artist that had recently died. The contract price was $100000 in cash payable one month after a truck carrier delivered the painting to the collector. The painting was damaged in transit. The collector timely rejected it after inspection and immediately notified the gallery of the rejection. The gallery then sold the painting to a third party. It informed the collector that it would pick up the painting within a couple of weeks. Two weeks later before the gallery picked up the painting the collector sold the painting to an art admirer for $120000 cash after notifying her about the damage. If the collector's sale of the painting was NOT an acceptance of the goods what is the maximum amount that the gallery is entitled to recover from the collector?

Choices:
A. $120000 (damages for conversion).
B. $100000 (the collector-gallery contract price).
C. $20000 (the excess of the market price over the contract price).
D. Only the allowance of lost profit to the gallery as a volume dealer.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Conversion under the UCC, specifically the wrongful exercise of ownership over goods after rightful rejection.

Fact Analysis: The collector initially rejected the damaged painting upon inspection and notified the gallery, but then sold the painting to a third party for $120,000 before the gallery could retrieve it. This action occurred after the gallery had already disposed of the painting by selling it to another party.

Rule Application: Under the UCC, a buyer's exercise of ownership over goods after rightful rejection can constitute conversion, entitling the seller to the fair market value of the goods at the time of conversion. The remedy for conversion is not limited to the contract price, especially when the seller is not a lost volume seller, as in the case of a one-of-a-kind good.

Legal Conclusion: Given the collector's wrongful exercise of ownership by selling the painting after its initial rejection, the gallery is entitled to the fair market value of the painting at the time of conversion, which is evidenced by the collector's sale price of $120,000. Therefore, the gallery can recover $120,000 from the collector, supporting option A.

On March 1 an excavator entered into a contract with a contractor to perform excavation work on a large project. The contract expressly required that the excavator begin work on June 1 to enable other subcontractors to install utilities. On May 15 the excavator requested a 30-day delay in the start date for the excavation work because he was seriously behind schedule on another project. When the contractor refused to grant the delay the excavator stated that he would try to begin the work for the contractor on June 1. Does the contractor have valid legal grounds to cancel the contract with the excavator and hire a replacement?

Choices:
A. Yes because the excavator committed an anticipatory repudiation of the contract by causing the contractor to feel insecure about the performance.
B. Yes because the excavator breached the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
C. No because the excavator would be entitled to specific performance of the contract if he could begin by June 1.
D. No because the excavator did not state unequivocally that he would delay the beginning of his work.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Anticipatory repudiation in contract law, specifically the conditions under which a party's statement or action may be considered a repudiation of their contractual obligations.

Fact Analysis: The excavator requested a 30-day delay in the start date for the excavation work due to being behind schedule on another project, but after the contractor's refusal, the excavator stated he would try to begin the work on the original start date of June 1.

Rule Application: For a statement or action to constitute an anticipatory repudiation, it must unequivocally manifest an intention not to perform or an inability to perform. A request for a delay or an expression of doubt about one's ability to perform does not meet this standard.

Legal Conclusion: Since the excavator's request for a delay and subsequent statement that he would try to begin work on June 1 do not unequivocally manifest an intention not to perform, the contractor does not have valid legal grounds to cancel the contract based on anticipatory repudiation, supporting option D.

On March 1 a mechanic contracted to repair a textile company's knitting machine by March 6. On March 2 the textile company contracted to manufacture and deliver specified cloth to a customer on March 15. The textile company knew that it would have to use the machine then under repair to perform this contract. Because the customer's order was for a rush job the two parties included in their contract a liquidated damages clause providing that the textile company would pay $5000 for each day's delay in delivery after March 15. The mechanic was inexcusably five days late in repairing the machine and as a result the textile company was five days late in delivering the cloth to the customer. The textile company paid $25000 to the customer as liquidated damages and then sued the mechanic for $25000. Both the mechanic and the textile company knew when making their contract on March 1 that under ordinary circumstances the textile company would sustain few or no damages of any kind as a result of a five-day delay in the machine repair. Assuming that the $5000-per-day liquidated damages clause in the contract between the textile company and the customer is valid which of the following arguments will serve as the mechanic's best defense to the textile company's action?

Choices:
A. Time was not of the essence in the contract between the mechanic and the textile company.
B. The mechanic had no reason to foresee on March 1 that the customer would suffer consequential damages in the amount of $25000.
C. By entering into the contract with the customer while knowing that its knitting machine was being repaired the textile company assumed the risk of any delay loss to the customer.
D. In all probability the liquidated damages paid by the textile company to the customer are not the same amount as the actual damages sustained by the customer in consequence of the late delivery of the cloth.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Consequential damages in contract law, specifically the requirement that such damages must be reasonably foreseeable to the breaching party.

Fact Analysis: The mechanic contracted to repair a textile company's knitting machine by March 6, but was inexcusably five days late. This delay caused the textile company to be late in delivering cloth to a customer, resulting in liquidated damages of $25000. The textile company and the mechanic knew that under ordinary circumstances, a five-day delay in machine repair would result in few or no damages.

Rule Application: Consequential damages are recoverable only if they were reasonably foreseeable to the breaching party. In this case, the textile company did not inform the mechanic of its contract with the customer, and thus the mechanic had no reason to know the impact of his delay on the textile company's relationship with its customer.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the mechanic had no reason to foresee the consequential damages resulting from his breach, the best defense to the textile company's action is that the mechanic had no reason to foresee on March 1 that the customer would suffer consequential damages in the amount of $25000, supporting option B.

A seller and a buyer entered into a written agreement providing that the seller was to deliver 1000 cases of candy bars to the buyer during the months of May and June. Under the agreement the buyer was obligated to make a selection by March 1 of the quantities of the various candy bars to be delivered under the contract. The buyer did not make the selection by March 1 and on March 2 the seller notified the buyer that because of the buyer's failure to select the seller would not deliver the candy bars. The seller had all of the necessary candy bars on hand on March 1 and made no additional sales or purchases on March 1 or March 2. On March 2 after receiving the seller's notice that it would not perform the buyer notified the seller of its selection and insisted that the seller perform. The seller refused. If the buyer sues the seller for breach of contract is the buyer likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No because a contract did not exist until selection of the specific candy bars and the seller withdrew its offer before selection.
B. No because selection of the candy bars by March 1 was an express condition to the seller's duty to perform.
C. Yes because a delay of one day in making the selection did not have a material effect on the seller.
D. Yes because upon the buyer's failure to make a selection by March 1 the seller had a duty to make a reasonable selection.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Buyer's duty to cooperate in specifying assortment of goods under UCC § 2-311 and the impact of failure to do so on the seller's performance.

Fact Analysis: The buyer failed to make a selection of candy bars by the agreed-upon date of March 1, prompting the seller to notify the buyer that it would not deliver the goods. The buyer then made a selection on March 2, but the seller refused to perform.

Rule Application: Under UCC § 2-311, a buyer's failure to specify the assortment of goods can be treated as a breach only if it materially impacts the seller's performance. In this case, the seller had an available supply of candy bars and had not entered into any new contracts, indicating that the buyer's delay in selection did not have a material effect on the seller's performance.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the buyer's failure to select did not materially impact the seller's performance, the seller's refusal to accept the buyer's selection on March 2 was unjustified. Therefore, the buyer is likely to prevail in a suit for breach of contract, supporting option C.

Before putting her home up for sale a homeowner painted the living room ceiling to conceal major water damage caused by a leaking roof that had not yet been repaired. On the first day the home was offered for sale the homeowner gave a buyer a personal tour. The homeowner made no statements at all regarding the water damage or the roof. Without discovering the water damage or the leaking roof and without consulting a lawyer the buyer immediately agreed in writing to buy the home for $200000. Before the closing date the buyer discovered the water damage and the leaking roof. The cost of repair was estimated at $22000. The buyer has refused to go through with the purchase. If the homeowner sues the buyer for breach of contract is the homeowner likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No because no contract was formed since the buyer did not have a real opportunity to understand the essential terms of the contract.
B. No because the homeowner concealed evidence of the water damage and of the leaking roof.
C. Yes because the homeowner made no affirmative statements of fact about the water damage or the leaking roof.
D. Yes because the buyer acted unreasonably by failing to employ an inspector to conduct an independent inspection of the home.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Misrepresentation of fact in contract law, specifically the concept of affirmative conduct intended to conceal or prevent discovery of a material fact.

Fact Analysis: The homeowner painted over the water damage on the living room ceiling before showing the house to the buyer, making no statements about the damage or the leaking roof. The buyer agreed to purchase the home without discovering the water damage or consulting a lawyer, only to later discover the issue and refuse to complete the purchase.

Rule Application: A misrepresentation of fact that induces assent provides a basis for avoidance of a contract. Affirmative conduct intended to prevent another from learning a fact is equivalent to an assertion that the fact does not exist and constitutes a misrepresentation. The homeowner's actions in painting over the water damage fall under this rule.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the homeowner's affirmative conduct was intended to conceal the water damage and the leaking roof, thereby inducing the buyer's assent, the buyer can avoid the contract. Therefore, the homeowner is unlikely to prevail in a suit for breach of contract, supporting option B.

A wholesaler contracted in a signed writing to sell to a bakery 10000 pounds of flour each week for 10 weeks the flour to be delivered to the bakery on Mondays and payment to be made on Wednesdays of each week. The bakery did all of its weekly bread baking on Tuesdays. On Monday morning of the first week the wholesaler tendered delivery of 8000 pounds of flour to the bakery and the bakery accepted it on the wholesaler's assurance that the remaining 2000 pounds would be delivered later that evening which it was. The bakery paid for both deliveries on Wednesday. On Monday of the second week the wholesaler tendered delivery of 5000 pounds of flour to the bakery and said that the remaining 5000 pounds could not be delivered on Monday but would be delivered by Wednesday. The bakery rejected the tender. Was the bakery legally justified in rejecting the tender of the 5000 pounds of flour?

Choices:
A. Yes because the bakery was legally entitled to reject any tender that did not conform perfectly to the contract.
B. Yes because the tender was a substantial impairment of that installment and could not be cured.
C. No because the tender was not a substantial impairment of the entire contract and the wholesaler had given assurance of a cure.
D. No because by accepting the first 8000 pounds on Monday of the first week the bakery had waived the condition of perfect tender and had not reinstated it.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Perfect tender rule under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), specifically the right of a buyer to reject nonconforming installments.

Fact Analysis: The wholesaler contracted to deliver 10000 pounds of flour to the bakery each week for 10 weeks, with delivery on Mondays and payment on Wednesdays. In the second week, the wholesaler tendered only 5000 pounds, stating the remaining 5000 pounds would be delivered by Wednesday, which would be after the bakery's weekly baking needs.

Rule Application: Under UCC § 2-612(2), a buyer may reject any nonconforming installment if the nonconformity substantially impairs the value of that installment and cannot be cured. The delay in delivery of the remaining 5000 pounds until Wednesday would substantially impair the value of the installment for the bakery's weekly baking needs.

Legal Conclusion: Given the substantial impairment of the installment's value due to the delayed delivery and the inability to cure, the bakery was legally justified in rejecting the tender of the 5000 pounds of flour, supporting option B.

An experienced rancher contracted to harvest his neighbor's wheat crop for $1000 "when the crop [was] ripe." In early September the neighbor told the rancher that the crop was ripe. The rancher delayed because he had other customers to attend to. The neighbor was concerned that the delay might cause the crop to be lost for hailstorms were common in that part of the country in the fall. In fact in early October before the crop was harvested it was destroyed by a hailstorm. Is the rancher liable for the loss?

Choices:
A. No because no time for performance was established in the contract.
B. No because the neighbor failed to tell the rancher that the crop might be destroyed by a hailstorm.
C. Yes because at the time the contract was made the rancher had reason to foresee the loss as a probable result of his breach.
D. Yes because a party who undertakes a contractual obligation is liable for all the consequences that flow from his breach.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Contract law, specifically the recoverability of damages for a breach of contract and the foreseeability of loss.

Fact Analysis: The rancher contracted to harvest the neighbor's wheat crop for $1000 when the crop was ripe. The neighbor informed the rancher the crop was ripe in early September, but the rancher delayed, and the crop was destroyed by a hailstorm in early October. The rancher's experience and the frequency of hailstorms in the fall are relevant circumstances.

Rule Application: According to the Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 351, a non-breaching party is entitled to recover damages that the party in breach had reason to foresee as a probable result of the breach when the parties entered into the contract. The rancher's experience and the frequency of hailstorms in the fall combined to make the loss resulting from the rancher's breach foreseeable.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the rancher had reason to foresee the loss as a probable result of his breach, he is liable for the loss. Therefore, the correct answer is C, as the rancher's experience and the frequency of hailstorms in the fall made the loss foreseeable, supporting his liability for the loss.

A niece had worked in her aunt's bookstore for many years. The bookstore business which was housed in a building that the aunt leased was independently appraised at $200000. The aunt decided to retire. She wrote to the niece expressing her affection for the niece and offering to sell her the bookstore business for $125000 if the landlord would agree to a transfer of the lease. The letter also specified when the aunt would transfer the business. The niece wrote back accepting her aunt's offer. In a phone call to the niece the aunt stated that the landlord had approved the transfer of the lease and that she would now ask her attorney to draft a written contract so that there would be a record of the terms. Before the attorney had finished drafting the document the aunt changed her mind about selling the business and informed the niece of her decision. In an action for breach of contract brought by the niece against her aunt is the niece likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No because the motivation for the transfer of the business was the aunt's affection for her niece not the price.
B. No because the promised consideration was inadequate in light of the market value of the business.
C. Yes because the condition concerning the landlord's assent to the transfer of the lease was beyond the control of either party.
D. Yes because the document being drafted by the attorney was merely a record of an agreement already made not a condition to it.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Formation of a contract, specifically the role of written documentation in contract formation and the effect of a party's change of mind.

Fact Analysis: The aunt offered to sell her bookstore business to the niece for $125,000, contingent on the landlord agreeing to transfer the lease. The niece accepted the offer, and the aunt informed the niece that the landlord had approved the transfer and would ask her attorney to draft a written contract. However, before the contract was finalized, the aunt changed her mind about selling the business.

Rule Application: A contract is formed when there is a valid offer, acceptance, and consideration. The fact that the parties intended to create a written document does not mean that the contract was not formed until the document was signed. If the terms of the contract were agreed upon and the only remaining step was the preparation of a written document, the contract is enforceable despite the absence of a written agreement.

Legal Conclusion: In this case, the aunt's offer and the niece's acceptance formed a binding contract, regardless of the aunt's subsequent change of mind. The fact that the attorney was drafting a written contract merely served as a record of the agreement already made, rather than a condition to its formation. Therefore, the niece is likely to prevail in her action for breach of contract, supporting option D.

A buyer sent a seller an offer to buy 50 tons of cotton of a specified quality. The offer contained no terms except those specifying the amount and quality of the cotton. The seller then sent an acknowledgment by fax. The acknowledgment repeated the terms of the buyer's offer and stated that shipment would occur within five days. Among 12 printed terms on the acknowledgment was a statement that any dispute about the cotton's quality would be submitted to arbitration. Neither the buyer nor the seller said anything further about arbitration. The seller shipped the cotton and it was accepted by the buyer. A dispute arose between the buyer and the seller as to the quality of the cotton and the seller asserted that the dispute had to be submitted to arbitration. The buyer instead sued the seller in court. In that suit which of the following arguments best supports the seller's position that the buyer must submit the dispute to arbitration?

Choices:
A. Arbitration is a more efficient method of resolving disputes than resolving them in court.
B. The provision for arbitration did not contradict any term in the buyer's offer.
C. The provision for arbitration did not materially alter the parties' contract.
D. The seller's acknowledgment containing a provision for arbitration constituted a counteroffer that was accepted by the buyer when it accepted delivery of the cotton.

Legal Concept: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 2-207(2) and its application to additional terms in contracts, particularly the provision for arbitration in a contract for the sale of goods.

Rule Application: Under UCC § 2-207(2), an additional term in a contract, such as the arbitration provision, is considered a proposal for addition to the contract. This additional term becomes part of the contract unless it materially alters the parties' contract. The arbitration provision will be considered a term of the contract if it does not materially alter the parties' contract.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the arbitration provision did not contradict any term in the buyer's offer and its inclusion did not fundamentally change the nature of the agreement, it is reasonable to argue that the provision did not materially alter the parties' contract. Which of the following statements is most accurate with respect to the breach of contract claim against the janitorial service?

The patient, who was not a party to the contract, contracted an infection due to the janitorial service's failure to meet the hygiene standards, leading to a breach of contract claim against the janitorial service.

This is determined by factors such as identification in the contract, direct receipt of performance, or a relationship indicating an intent to benefit. In this case, the patient does not meet these criteria, as the contract was between the hospital and the janitorial service without explicit intent to benefit the patient.

Legal Conclusion: Given the analysis, the patient is considered an incidental beneficiary rather than an intended third-party beneficiary. Therefore, the patient has no claim for breach of contract against the janitorial service, supporting option C.

On June 1 a general contractor and a subcontractor entered into a contract under which the subcontractor agreed to deliver all of the steel joists that the general contractor required in the construction of a hospital building. Although the general contractor had no reason to doubt the subcontractor's ability to perform the general contractor wanted to be sure that the subcontractor was on track for delivery in September. He therefore wrote a letter on July 1 to the subcontractor demanding that the subcontractor provide assurance of its ability to meet the September 1 deadline. The subcontractor refused to provide such assurance. The general contractor then immediately obtained the steel joists from another supplier. If the subcontractor sues the general contractor for breach of contract is the subcontractor likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No because the subcontractor anticipatorily repudiated the contract when it failed to provide adequate assurance.
B. No because the contract failed to specify a definite quantity.
C. Yes because a demand for assurance constitutes a breach of contract when the contract does not expressly authorize a party to demand assurance.
D. Yes because the subcontractor's failure to provide assurance was not a repudiation since there were no reasonable grounds for the general contractor's insecurity.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Adequate assurance doctrine in contract law, specifically the conditions under which a demand for assurance of performance is justified.

Fact Analysis: The general contractor, despite having no reason to doubt the subcontractor's ability to perform, demanded assurance of the subcontractor's ability to meet the September 1 delivery deadline. The subcontractor refused to provide such assurance, leading the general contractor to obtain the steel joists from another supplier.

Rule Application: Under the adequate assurance doctrine, a demand for assurance is justified only if the party making the demand has reasonable grounds for insecurity regarding the other party's potential performance. Since the general contractor had no reason to doubt the subcontractor's ability to perform, the demand for assurance was unjustified, and the subcontractor was not obligated to respond.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the general contractor's demand for assurance was unjustified and the subcontractor properly refused to respond, the subcontractor's failure to provide assurance did not constitute a repudiation of the contract. Therefore, the subcontractor is likely to prevail in a suit for breach of contract, supporting option D.

A seller entered into a contract to sell to a buyer a house for a price of $150000. The contract contained the following clause: "This contract is conditional on the buyer's securing bank financing at an interest rate of 7% or below." The buyer did not make an application for bank financing and therefore did not secure it and refused to proceed with the purchase. The seller sued the buyer for breach of contract. Is the seller likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No because the buyer did not secure bank financing.
B. No because the contract did not expressly impose on the buyer any obligation to apply for bank financing.
C. Yes because a court will excuse the condition to avoid a disproportionate forfeiture.
D. Yes because a court will imply a term imposing on the buyer a duty to use reasonable efforts to secure bank financing.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Conditions in contracts, specifically the duty of good faith and fair dealing in relation to express conditions.

Fact Analysis: The contract between the seller and buyer contained a condition that the buyer secure bank financing at an interest rate of 7% or below. The buyer did not apply for bank financing and refused to proceed with the purchase.

Rule Application: According to the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, every contract imposes a duty of good faith and fair dealing in its performance and enforcement. This duty implies that the buyer must make reasonable efforts to secure bank financing, as the condition's nonoccurrence does not discharge the buyer's performance obligation without such efforts.

Legal Conclusion: Given the implied duty of good faith, the buyer's failure to make reasonable efforts to secure bank financing means the seller is likely to prevail in a breach of contract suit, supporting option D.

A computer retail outlet contracted to service a bank's computer equipment for one year at a fixed monthly fee under a contract that was silent as to assignment or delegation by either party. Three months later the retail outlet sold the service portion of its business to an experienced and well-financed computer service company. The only provision in the agreement between the retail outlet and the computer service company relating to the outlet's contract with the bank stated that the outlet "hereby assigns all of its computer service contracts to [the computer service company]." The computer service company performed the monthly maintenance required under the service contract. Its performance was defective however and caused damage to the bank's operations. Whom can the bank sue for damages arising from the computer service company's defective performance?

Choices:
A. The retail outlet only because the computer service company made no promises to the bank.
B. Either the retail outlet or the computer service company because the bank has not released the outlet and the bank is an intended beneficiary of the outlet's agreement with the computer service company.
C. Either the retail outlet or the computer service company because since each has the right to enforce the bank's performance of its contract with the retail outlet mutuality of remedy renders either potentially liable for the defective performance.
D. The computer service company only because it is a qualified and a financially responsible supplier of computer services.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Delegation of duties and assignment of rights in contract law, specifically the liability of the delegating party and the delegatee to the obligee.

Fact Analysis: The retail outlet contracted with the bank for computer equipment service and later sold the service portion of its business to the computer service company, assigning all its computer service contracts. The computer service company performed the contract but defectively, causing damage to the bank's operations.

Rule Application: A delegation of duties does not relieve the delegating party of its obligations to the obligee without the obligee's consent or the delegatee's performance. Additionally, when the delegatee agrees to perform the delegating party's obligations, the obligee becomes an intended beneficiary of the delegatee's promise. In this case, both the retail outlet and the computer service company remain liable to the bank for defective performance.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the bank did not consent to the delegation and the computer service company's performance was defective, the bank can sue either the retail outlet or the computer service company for damages, as both parties remain liable.
